How Hammel Works

Source: vignettes/articles/how_it_works.qmd

Event Scheduling

SOCSIM Approach

To understand the approach Hammel takes to event scheduling, it is useful to understand how SOCSIM worked, as Hammel is built on the same principles.

For each living individual in the population, SOCSIM calculates waiting time until the next event for each kind of rate process (e.g. death, birth, marriage, transition). This is first accomplished by drawing a value from rexp(1) for each rate process which provides a measure of the risk that someone will accumulate before the event happens. SOCSIM then advances through a persons’ age or duration specific bands (and also possibly joint time bands for time-varying rates) and the hazard rate within each band consumes that accumulated risk. If accumulated risk remains then SOCSIM moves on to the next band and so on, until the accumulated risk is completely consumed. The time to event within the final band can be determined by \(R/\lambda\) where \(R\) is the remaining accumulated risk at the start of this band and \(\lambda\) is the hazard rate in this band.

Notably, this approach provides an exact time to event and does not require the discrete month-based approach that SOCSIM instead uses, likely for historical reasons. In any case, SOCSIM truncates these event times to months of time.

SOCSIM then chooses the nearest event (dealing with some tie issues due to month truncation) and adds it to an event queue. Events are processed off the queue in monthly batches and new events are then scheduled (assuming the processed event wasn’t death in which case you don’t get any more events).

Hammel’s Approach

Initially, Hammel used the exact same approach as SOCSIM with one important modification. We dropped the discrete monthly approach and moved to a continuous time approach. This actually required no extra work because the process itself is better geared toward continuous time than a discrete time approach.

However, we eventually switched to a different approach that helped to address other engineering issues that had arisen in the course of development.

Individuals no longer draw individual waiting times to events. Instead, each rate process is given a single clock that determines the time to the next event for the population. Individuals/unions are then chosen to receive the event based on a multistage design that preserves the correct input rates.

For each rate process, we first create bins that distinguish every dimension by which the rate is stratified (e.g. age, duration, group membership, union type). Within bin \(i\), we have a \(\lambda_i\) individual hazard rate that is directly determined by the input rate schedule. We also track \(N_i\), which is the number of people in the simulation who currently occupy that bin. We can then get the total hazard rate \(\gamma_i\) for that bin by:

\[\gamma_i = \lambda_iN_i\]

We can then calculate \(\gamma\), the collective risk of the next event, by taking the sum of the \(\gamma_i\):

\[\gamma = \sum_i \gamma_i\]

We can then determine the waiting time until the next event in the entire population by taking \(E/\gamma\) where \(E\) is a draw from rexp(1). If \(\gamma\) changes before the event is executed, whether because people move between bins or because rates change at a calendar boundary, we recalculate the remaining waiting time \(t\) by taking:

\[t_{new} = t_{old} \frac{\gamma_{old}}{\gamma_{new}}\]

If a calendar boundary changes the structure of bins themselves, the process is rebuilt and draws a new waiting time, which is equally valid because exponential waiting times are memoryless.

When an event occurs, we then choose which bin it occurs within by sampling from bins weighted by their \(\gamma_i\). Within each bin, we then draw a random person/union, possibly with weights that are discussed below. Then the process produces a new waiting time and the cycle continues.

The computationally intensive part of this process is managing the \(N_i\) values. While individuals don’t produce individual waiting times, they do move between these bins. In many cases, moving between a bin happens when another event occurs to that person/union. For example, if a woman marries, in any rate that is stratified by union type, she will move from the unpartnered bin to the partnered bin. The other major bookkeeping is tracking when a person or union hits a band edge because this will move them into a new bin. For example, if the mortality age bands are 30-35 and 35-40, a person will hit a band edge on their 35th birthday.

We chose this process not because it simplified the code base or decreased runtime. In some cases, this approach is faster than our previous approach, but in other cases, it is slower. The main reason for adopting this approach was to deal with a specific problem with fertility and because it opened up the possibility to fully develop weights that allow for flexible proportional hazards.

Resolving the birth interval issue

The complication with fertility is that birth intervals between births mean that fewer person-years of life are actually spent exposed to the risk of giving birth than standard fertility rates imply. Our original approach to this issue at the individual level was similar to SOCSIM’s approach - we used an approximation to boost the fertility rates we actually use to compensate for this issue. This approximation works well in many cases, but can fail when there is fertility change within a single simulation or across restarts. It also fails badly for parity-specific fertility.

The binned approach resolves this issue fairly neatly. We distinguish \(N_i\) for fertility which is all women from the actual number of eligible women within the bin (those not within the birth interval of a previous birth). We sample only among eligible women. With this approach, we do not have to make any adjustment to the input rates. We also always use fine-grained one year age intervals and one birth parity intervals when constructing bins for fertility rates even when the given bands are larger, because lack of eligibility will shift risk over to other women in the bin. With wide age or parity bins, this could shift risk to women of substantially different age or parity.

One potential issue may arise with this approach. It is possible to have \(N_i > 0\) in a bin but no eligible women. When this bin is sampled, there will be no women to produce a birth. In these cases, we record an unrealized birth in the final output. Overall fertility will be somewhat underestimated. This situation will be rare except for simulations with small active populations and very fine bins. We have found it most noticeable at high parity-low age bins when using parity-specific births because relatively few women will be in these bins and most of them will have recently given birth.

Weighting individual sampling within bins

To allow for complex variation in the hazard rates of individuals/unions in a parsimonious manner, we introduced the concept of a weight model that can be applied to any rate process. The weight model creates a weight for each individual within a bin. This weight is used to decide who to sample from the bin.

The weight model allows users to specify models on the log-weight using formulas or a custom function. This approach effectively creates a proportional hazard model. For example, here is a simple weight model that uses a weight of 1.2 for members of some group B:

weight_model(~group, coefficients = c("groupB" = log(1.2)))

Because members of group B receive a weight of 1.2 compared to 1 for all other groups across all bins, their observed rates will be 20% higher than for other groups, within each bin.

Because this model only affects the sampling within bins, the overall input rates will be preserved in the output. This approach allows users to use a simple overall rate schedule, while allowing for complex proportional hazards that may not even be possible using stratified rates.

However, users should be aware of one potential limitation of this approach. If the distribution of covariates that affect the proportional hazards shifts over time, this will come out as changes in the hazard across those covariates, not in the overall rate. For example, if the example above involved two groups A and B and B shrank as a share of the population, to maintain the overall hazard, the hazard rate of both groups would have to increase. If B increased as a share of the population, the hazard rate of both groups would have to decrease. In contrast, if stratified rates by group with a 20% fixed difference are used instead, then the group-specific hazard rates would stay constant but the overall hazard rate would have to change. Depending on the goals of a simulation, either one of these approaches can work, but users should be aware of how the process works.

Also, because bins are stratified by the rate schedules, weights within bin among characteristics that are already used for stratification will have no effect. For example, if a user provides rates stratified by group, then weighting by group will have no effect because the weights will be identical within each bin.

Weighted choice in union formation

Matching partners uses a conditional logit model in which women pick men by weights that derive from, for example, age differences and group exogamy. However, because women do the choosing, the results for group assignment will be asymmetric by gender. We apply a group-based weight to each potential husband to correct for this issue. Below we detail the rationale and describe how this weight is constructed in the program.

A Simplified Scenario

Imagine a population of A and B individuals where A is 75% of the population and B is 25% of the population and everyone is married at once in a large “marriage jubilee.” Let’s assume that there was no group-specific preference for marriage partners. We would then expect the distribution of couple types by group to match that shown in Table 1.

Now let’s assume a conditional logit process where women choose from among available men with a log-odds discount of \(\beta\) (where \(\beta\) < 0) such that if she was comparing one man from the same group and one man from the other group the probability of an endogamous choice would be \(1/(1+e^{\beta})\) and the probability of an exogamous choice would be \(e^{\beta}/(1+e^{\beta})\). Considering that the woman will be presented with different distributions of men by group, the overall probabilities need to be adjusted by group size:

\[P(\text{A woman chooses A man}) = \frac{0.75}{0.75 + 0.25e^{\beta}} = \frac{0.75}{D_A}\] \[P(\text{A woman chooses B man}) = \frac{0.25e^{\beta}}{0.75 + 0.25e^{\beta}} = \frac{0.25e^{\beta}}{D_A}\] \[P(\text{B woman chooses A man}) = \frac{0.75e^{\beta}}{0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}} = \frac{0.75e^{\beta}}{D_B}\] \[P(\text{B woman chooses B man}) = \frac{0.25}{0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}} = \frac{0.25}{D_B}\]

Where, \(D_A = 0.75 + 0.25 e^{\beta}\) and \(D_B = 0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}\). These denominators represent the sum of all of the exponentiated utilities for a given woman (i.e. the overall attractiveness of her pool) which is used to normalize the probabilities for each type of woman across partner choices.

To get the value of each cell in the table correct we then multiply by the row share of A and B women as shown in Table 2.

The inverse cross product of Table 2 gives us the association odds ratio often used in assortative mating studies:

\[\frac{(0.25)(0.75)e^{\beta}D_B^{-1}(0.75)(0.25)e^{\beta}D_A^{-1}}{(0.75)(0.75)D_A^{-1}(0.25)(0.25)D_B^{-1}} = e^{2\beta}\]

Everything cancels out except for the \(\beta\) values. The log cross product is thus \(2\beta\) which is consistent with conditional logit model estimates typically around half the log-odds ratio in empirical data. If we set \(\beta = 0\) here, then \(D_A = 1\) and \(D_B = 1\) and Table 2 simplifies to Table 1.

Although the overall log-odds ratio matches expectation here, the counts of A wives and B husbands (\(N_AB\)) and B wives and A husbands (\(N_BA\)) are not balanced despite gender balance within each group:

\[\frac{N_{AB}}{N_{BA}} = \frac{(0.75)(0.25)e^{\beta}D_A^{-1}}{(0.25)(0.75)e^{\beta}D_B^{-1}} = \frac{D_B}{D_A} = \frac{0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}}{0.75 + 0.25 e^{\beta}}\]

This ratio can be substantially different from one. For example, at \(\beta = -3\), the ratio is 0.377 AB unions for every one BA union. Given that the model here assumes that the exogamy parameter is symmetric with regard to sex, this discrepancy is large.

The row marginals will add up to the overall distribution for women:

\[N_{A+} = \frac{(0.75)(0.75)+(0.75)(0.25)e^{\beta}}{0.75 + 0.25 e^{\beta}} = \frac{(0.75)(0.75 + 0.25e^{\beta})}{0.75 + 0.25 e^{\beta}} = 0.75\] \[N_{B+} = \frac{(0.25)(0.25) + (0.25)(0.75)e^{\beta}}{0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}} = \frac{(0.25)(0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta})}{0.25 + 0.75e^{\beta}} = 0.25\]

However, the column margins will not add up in the same way for men, because the two cells on each column do not share a single denominator. For example, in the case with \(\beta = -3\), group B men will only make up 0.2298 of husbands as opposed to the 0.25 for women.

The underlying issue is that because women drive the choices we don’t observe a symmetric process. If we switched to having men do the choosing, we would observe the same issues but in the reverse direction.

Applying a weight correction

We can generalize this approach by setting \(F_i\) and \(M_j\) as the share of women and men respectively belonging to a certain group (0.75 and 0.25 for groups A and B, respectively, in the example above) and setting utility \(U_{ij}\) as:

\[ U_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = j \\ \beta & \text{if } i \neq j \end{cases} \]

Then, the value of \(N_{ij}\) in cell \(ij\) is given by:

\[N_{ij} = F_i \cdot \frac{M_j e^{U_{ij}}}{D_i}, \qquad D_i = \sum_k M_k e^{U_{ik}}\]

It will be helpful to note how this approach compares to the typical log-linear formulation:

Where \(r_i\) and \(c_i\) are row and column scores estimated to ensure the correct marginal distributions. This approach will produce the same \(\beta\) value and when the male and female group distributions are the same it will also produce \(N_{AB} = N_{BA}\). We can reproduce this approach directly while maintaining the conditional logit model method by applying a group-specific weight to each man.

Intuitively, these weights act like a “price adjustment” to modify the attractiveness of group B men so their column share matches the desired 25%. It does not modify the odds ratio but rather just the ratio of \(N_{AB}\) to \(N_{BA}\).

With weights \(\omega_j\) on men of group \(j\), we can modify the previous formula for the cell counts to:

\[N_{ij} = F_i \cdot \frac{\omega_j M_j e^{U_{ij}}}{D_i}, \qquad D_i = \sum_k \omega_k M_k e^{U_{ik}}\]

A slight reformulation here gives us:

\[N_{ij} = \frac{F_i}{D_i} \cdot \omega_j M_j \cdot e^{U_{ij}}\]

This is exactly the log-linear form \(r_i c_j e^{U_{ij}}\), with

\[r_i = \frac{F_i}{D_i}, \qquad c_j = \omega_j M_j\]

In this simplified two group example, there is a closed form analytical solution to solve for \(\omega_j\). First, we set \(\omega_A = 1\) as the reference weight. Then we define \(f\) as the share of women in group A, \(p\) as the share of men in group A, and \(q = 1 - p\) as the share of men in group B. Table 4 shows the equations governing the joint distribution of spouses.

The constraint is that \(N_{AB}+N_{BB} = q\). Solving for that constraint gives a quadratic form:

\[ qe^{\beta}\omega_B^2+\underbrace{\left[p-f+(f-q)e^{2\beta}\right]}_{C}\omega_B-pe^{\beta}=0 \]

We can solve for the positive root of the quadratic to get the analytical solution for \(\omega_B\):

\[ \omega_B = \frac{\sqrt{C^2 + 4pq\,e^{2\beta}} - C}{2q\,e^\beta}, \qquad C = p - f + (f - q)e^{2\beta}. \]

Notably, this solution forces the following equality:

\[N_{AB} - N_{BA} = f - p\]

When the groups have the same share within each gender, \(f-p = 0\) and we will have symmetry in \(N_{AB} = N_{BA}\).

Table 5 shows the cell counts, log odds ratio and AB/BA ratio under different input scenarios where the group share within each gender is the same. All scenarios produce a log odds ratio that is exactly double the input \(\beta\). When A and B are equal shares of the population, the weighted and unweighted results are identical. When A is 75% of each gender, then the results diverge substantially. The unweighted results (i.e. \(\omega_B = 1\)) will produce almost a 3:1 ratio of B woman/A man pairings compared to A woman/B man pairings. The weighted results produce equal number of AB and BA pairings.

One limitation of this approach is that it does not allow for directional differences by gender in the ratio - the exogamy parameter \(\beta\) must be symmetric with regard to sex. In many cases, this will be appropriate as a single marker of group boundaries, but some empirical cases may have a clear difference in intermarriage likelihood by gender, suggesting that men and women of that group are viewed differently as partners. For example, research has shown about a 3:1 disparity in black men/white women compared to white men/black women pairings in the US.

Another issue is demonstrated in Table 6. When group shares are not the same by gender, even fairly minor differences can produce even larger gender disparity than in the unweighted approach. This is because of the equality \(N_{AB} - N_{BA} = f - p\). This gender disparity must come out as a difference between the two cells. When intermarriage is less likely, the ratio will be even larger.

One way to help users address both of these issues is to use a tuning parameter \(\delta_g\) for each group. This parameter adjusts the general preference for husbands of this group relative to wives, such that \(\delta_g > 0\) gives a relative preference for husbands and \(\delta_g < 0\) gives a relative preference for wives.

This parameter will adjust the targeted constraint for \(N_{AB} + N_{BB}\) from \(q\) to:

\[\tau_B = \frac{qe^{\delta_B}}{p+qe^{\delta_B}}\]

Assuming \(\delta_A = 0\), the closed form solution for \(\omega_B\) becomes:

\[ \omega_B = \frac{p}{q} \frac{\sqrt{C^2 + 4\tau_B(1-\tau_B)e^{2\beta}} - C} {2(1-\tau_B)e^\beta}, \qquad C = (f-\tau_B)e^{2\beta} + 1-f-\tau_B \]

Table 7 shows scenarios using the \(\delta\) tuning parameter. The first three rows show a case with even group share by sex in which the tuning parameter is used to create either a roughly 3:1 or 1:3 ratio of AB to BA unions. The last three rows show using the tuning parameter to adjust the ratio from a case of uneven group share by sex to either 1:1 or 1:3.

How this approach is implemented

Together, the \(\omega\) weights and the \(\delta\) tuning parameters give us considerable control over intergroup exogamy while retaining the computationally efficient conditional logit approach. Implementing this approach in the simulation is, however, more complicated than the static two-group case developed above.

In the simulation, women start searches one at a time, at different times, so there is no single “jubilee” to balance. Calibration instead balances the flow of matches. At the moment of each search, it solves for male-group weights that would give the right expected distribution of husbands, if every woman currently at risk of searching were to search. The focal woman then chooses using those weights. Calibration involves no random draws.

Calibration tracks living, unpartnered men and women at or above the minimum male age. They are classified by group and by quarter-year birth cohort. With several group dimensions, a “group” is a person’s combination of categories in the dimensions that matching uses.

Each counted woman contributes her current hazard of starting a partner search, \(\lambda_w\):

  • for marriage and cohabitation searches in rate mode, we use her union formation hazard.
  • for searches triggered by a birth (on-demand formation) and for choosing nonmarital fathers, we use her fertility hazard. A woman within her birth interval contributes zero.

These contributions are kept as running totals by group and cohort, updated whenever a woman moves between rate cells, crosses a band edge or leaves the pool, so they are always current. Each kind of search is calibrated separately with its own matching model.

For male targets, let \(r_g\) be the total search intensity of group \(g\)’s women divided by their number. Men are given the same average intensity as the women of their own group: if \(M_g\) is the number of counted men in group \(g\), the target share of husbands from group \(g\) is

\[\tau_g = \frac{M_g, r_g, e^{\delta_g}}{\sum_h M_h, r_h, e^{\delta_h}}\]

A group with no counted women uses the population-wide average intensity for its men. The targets decide only which male groups the matches go to. Women’s search timing still decides how many matches occur.

For each woman, the calibration needs the sum of \(e^{U_{ij}}\) over the available men of each group, where \(U_{ij}\) is the utility between woman \(i\) and a given man \(j\). These sums are kept up to date as men enter and leave the pool. They are evaluated at cohort-center ages, and kin are not removed. Given a set of weights \(\omega\), these sums give each woman’s chance of choosing a husband from each group. Averaging those chances over all counted women, with each woman weighted by her search intensity, gives the expected share of husbands from each group. This is the general version of the column total \(N_{AB} + N_{BB}\) in the two-group example.

The \(\omega\) weights are found by Newton’s method so that the expected share of husbands from each group equals its target \(\tau_g\), starting from the previous search’s weights. One weight is fixed at 1, since only ratios matter. A group’s expected share rises steadily with its own weight, so when a solution exists it is unique.

The focal woman then chooses among her eligible men using exact ages, the full kinship screen and the calibrated weights:

\[P(j \mid w) = \frac{\omega_{g(j)}, e^{U_{wj}}}{\sum_{k} \omega_{g(k)}, e^{U_{wk}}}\]

Special cases.

  • With one group, or when exogamy is prohibited outright, every weight is 1 and the choice is ordinary female choice.
  • When prohibitions split the groups into blocks that cannot intermarry (for example, region = NA), each block is calibrated as its own marriage market. Its targets are scaled to its own women’s share of searching.
  • If a target can’t be reached, for instance because no compatible women are searching, the search uses the best available weights and is counted as approximate.
